explanations.explanation: Right on the money, friend. The text says it plainly: "Thus they forsook the LORD and did not serve Him." (Judges 10:6) To forsake is to walk away and leave Him behind. They had a whole crowd of gods to serve, and the LORD was the One they left out.

Good guess, because fear of the LORD is a real thing in Scripture. But this verse says the opposite is happening. The Israelites "forsook the LORD and did not serve Him." (Judges 10:6) Nobody in this verse is fearing Him. They're too busy serving the Baals and the Ashtoreths.

I wish it were praise, friend, I really do. But look at what the verse says: "Thus they forsook the LORD and did not serve Him." (Judges 10:6) The praise was going somewhere else. The Israelites were serving the Baals, the Ashtoreths and the gods of the nations around them.

That's the pair! The text says He "sold them into the hands of the Philistines and Ammonites." (Judges 10:7) The Philistines and Ammonites were neighboring nations. The LORD's anger burned, and these two were the hands Israel landed in.

Those two are real nations in the Bible, so I see why they came to mind. The Midianites are in Gideon's story earlier in Judges, but not here. Here the text says the LORD "sold them into the hands of the Philistines and Ammonites." (Judges 10:7) Keep those two names handy, because you'll hear them again.

Now those are some old names, friend. The Hittites and Jebusites are among the peoples who lived in the land long before. But in this passage the text says the LORD "sold them into the hands of the Philistines and Ammonites." (Judges 10:7) Different crowd this time.

Eighteen it is. The Philistines and Ammonites "harassed and oppressed the Israelites, and they did so for eighteen years." (Judges 10:8) That's a long stretch. Eighteen years of waiting makes a person count every single one.

Seven shows up in Judges, so that's a fair guess. The Midianites oppressed Israel for seven years in Gideon's day (Judges 6:1). This time the text says the oppression lasted "eighteen years." (Judges 10:8) That's more than double.

Forty is a big number in the Bible, so I get the pull. Judges does use it for some stretches of peace. Here, though, the text says the oppression went on "for eighteen years." (Judges 10:8) Long, but not forty.

Yes, they cry out. The text says, "Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD." (Judges 10:10) Israel was in deep distress, and the cry went up to the LORD. Sometimes that's all a person has left, and it's enough to start with.

Singing sounds nice, friend, and I'm a fan of a good song. But the verse says something rawer: "Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD." (Judges 10:10) They were in deep distress, so a cry fits. Not a song, a cry.

Showing up with a gift is a classic move, but that's not what the text says here. It says, "Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD." (Judges 10:10) Their hands were empty and their words were what they had. They came with a cry, and a confession right behind it.

I understand why that sounds right after what we just read. But He says the opposite. When those nations oppressed them and Israel cried out, He asks, "did I not save you from their hands?" (Judges 10:12) So the answer is False. In those earlier times, He saved them.

False is right. The LORD asks, "…you cried out to Me, did I not save you from their hands?" (Judges 10:12) He's reminding them that He saved them from the Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, Philistines, Sidonians, Amalekites and Maonites when they cried out. He didn't leave them in those hands.

That's the one, and it's a heavy line. The LORD says, "But you have forsaken Me and served other gods, so I will no longer save you." (Judges 10:13) That's what He tells them. I'm not going to hurry past it, friend, because it's a serious moment.

That would be a much easier verse to read, wouldn't it? But the LORD says, "But you have forsaken Me and served other gods, so I will no longer save you." (Judges 10:13) It's "no longer," not "always." I think that's a hard word to hear.

Quick rescue is what they were hoping for, I bet. But the LORD says, "But you have forsaken Me and served other gods, so I will no longer save you." (Judges 10:13) The word is "no longer." Quickly doesn't come into it.

Right, and they say it right out loud: "Deal with us as You see fit; but please deliver us today!" (Judges 10:15) They repeat their confession and put themselves in His hands. Then comes the ask for today. When you've been waiting a long time, I think you stop asking for later.

More time is the opposite of what they asked for. They'd already waited eighteen years (Judges 10:8). What they say is, "Deal with us as You see fit; but please deliver us today!" (Judges 10:15) They wanted deliverance, and they wanted it today.

A king would be a big ask, friend, and Israel does talk about kings in Judges. But that's not what they say to the LORD here. They say, "Deal with us as You see fit; but please deliver us today!" (Judges 10:15) Their request was to be delivered.

explanations.answer: They put them away and serve the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes! The text says, "So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD." (Judges 10:16) Their words were followed by action. The gods that had been sitting among them were put away.

explanations.answer: They hide them and keep serving them
explanations.explanation: Hiding something in the back of a closet is a very human move, I'll give you that. I know a thing or two about being shoved to the back of a drawer. But the text says, "So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD." (Judges 10:16) They put the gods away and served the LORD.

explanations.answer: They carry them along into battle
explanations.explanation: That would be a bold plan, but the text doesn't say it. It says, "So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD." (Judges 10:16) The foreign gods were put away. Nobody carried them anywhere.

True. After they put away the foreign gods and served the LORD, "He could no longer bear the misery of Israel." (Judges 10:16) That's a tender line. The LORD saw their misery and He couldn't stand by and bear it.

It's True, and I'm glad it is. The text says, "He could no longer bear the misery of Israel." (Judges 10:16) That comes right after they put away the foreign gods and served the LORD. It's a line worth coming back to.

explanations.answer: Head of all who live in Gilead
explanations.explanation: That's what they say. The rulers of Gilead tell one another, "Whoever will launch the attack against the Ammonites will be the head of all who live in Gilead." (Judges 10:18) Gilead was the land on the other side of the Jordan. The offer is leadership, and the Ammonites are waiting in the camp.

Land is a nice prize, friend, but the rulers don't promise it. They say, "Whoever will launch the attack against the Ammonites will be the head of all who live in Gilead." (Judges 10:18) The offer was about leading their own people.

Plunder is a big payday, so I see why you'd bet on it. But that's not the offer. The rulers say, "Whoever will launch the attack against the Ammonites will be the head of all who live in Gilead." (Judges 10:18) The reward was to be the head of Gilead.
